scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Mangambeu emerged in the early 1950s in Vendja-Bagangté, Ndé department.
It evolved from the Netchaa rhythm during the funeral wake of Mafeun Biatat.
The name honors a dancer, Dangmi Marie, whose performance was so striking that her praise-name was adopted for the style.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally born at a funeral, it is now used for births, weddings, and celebrations.
In Balengou and Bamena communities, it is called 'tchatcho' and celebrates people of exceptional achievement.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers move with small steps while swaying their hips.
The torso is frequently leaned forward.
It is a social dance performed by both men and women, characterized by rhythmic precision that matches the complex polyrhythms of the music.
Watch for Déhanchement.

Formation: Dancers evolve through the space using small steps

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is modal, usually oscillating between two chords.
It features a rhythmic superposition where the bass plays in 4/4 while xylophones and percussions play in 3/4 or 6/8.
Listen for the Xylophone (Mendzan), Sanza Mambala, Drums (Tam-tam), Electric Guitar.
The pulse is Polymetric (4/4 and 6/8) at about 110 beats a minute.
A dense, interlocking sound where a steady 4/4 pulse is challenged by rapid, triple-meter xylophone patterns and percussive accents.

Other key figures include the dancer Dangmi Marie, guitarist Jack Djeyim, and artists Daniel Njiké, Pierre Tchana, and Nya Directeur.
